h1: Wet hop beer and why India rarely sees it
title: Wet Hop Beer: Why India Rarely Sees It | Craft Beer School
desc: What wet hop beer is, why it tastes green and fresh plus the plain reasons it almost never appears on an Indian tap list.
teaser: Wet hop beer is brewed with hops picked that morning. India's hops travel for weeks, so here it is close to impossible.
standfirst: Most beer is made with dried hops pressed into pellets. Wet hop beer uses hops straight off the bine, unkilned and still full of water. It is a once a year beer. The reasons India almost never sees one say a lot about where our hops come from.
sections: Wet hops go from bine to kettle in a day

After picking, hops are normally dried in a kiln until their moisture falls to around 8 to 10%. Dry hops keep for months, especially once pressed into pellets and frozen. Wet hops skip the kiln entirely. They are picked and carried to the brewery as fast as possible, ideally within a day. They go into the kettle or the fermenter while still green and soft.

Freshly picked hops are about three quarters water. That means a brewer needs several times the weight of wet hops to match the aroma of dried ones, often quoted as four to six times as much. A recipe that would take 2 kg of pellets can need 10 kg of wet cones.

You will also see the term fresh hop. Brewers use it loosely, sometimes for wet hops and sometimes for hops that were kilned only days earlier.
The flavour is green, grassy and short lived

Wet hop beer does not taste like a big dry hopped IPA. It tends to be softer and greener, with notes of cut grass, fresh herbs and sometimes a light chlorophyll edge alongside the hop's usual fruit or pine. Drinkers who love it describe it as tasting like the hop garden.

That freshness fades within weeks. Wet hop beers are brewed to be drunk young, close to where they were made. If you are curious about how hops shape flavour more generally, our guide to hop varieties for beginners is a good next read.

Hops are harvested once a year. In the northern hemisphere, in the hop regions of the United States, Germany, the Czech Republic and England, picking runs from late August into September. In Australia and New Zealand it runs from about February to April.

That is why wet hop beers appear as a seasonal release in those countries. Breweries close to the hop farms book their share of the crop and brew on picking day. A brewery several hundred kilometres away has to move fast. One on another continent cannot do it at all.
A wet hop brew day is mostly about volume

Picture the brew day at a brewery near a hop farm. Sacks of green cones arrive in the afternoon, still warm from the field. Because the hops are so heavy with water, the brewer needs a lot of them. That bulk causes its own problems. Cones fill the kettle or the hop back, soak up wort and leave a mat of wet plant matter that has to be dug out by hand.

Most brewers add wet hops late: in the last minutes of the boil, in the whirlpool or in a hop back on the way to the heat exchanger. Boiling them for an hour would drive off the fresh character the whole exercise is about. Some also add wet hops to the fermenter, though the water and plant matter bring a higher risk of picking up bacteria from the field.

The yield is lower than a normal batch because the cones hold back so much wort. Breweries accept that for a beer they make once a year.
India has no commercial hop crop to speak of

Hops need long summer days, cold winters and a particular climate band, roughly between 35 and 55 degrees of latitude in either hemisphere. Most of India sits well south of that band. Nearly all the hops used by Indian breweries are imported as pellets or extract from the United States, Europe, Australia and New Zealand.

Wet hops spoil within a day or two. They begin to heat and rot in the sack because they are wet plant matter packed tight. A shipment that takes weeks to clear a port cannot arrive wet. Air freight would cost far more than the beer could carry. The hops would still need to clear customs and reach a brewery in hours.
What Indian drinkers can taste instead

There are a few ways to get close. Some breweries abroad freeze or vacuum pack freshly picked hops. Fresh crop pellets packed quickly after harvest carry bright aroma. An Indian brewery that buys new season pellets promptly and stores them frozen can release a beer that tastes noticeably fresher than one made with last year's stock.

Read the tap list in late autumn and in spring. A brewer who mentions new crop or fresh season hops is telling you something about care, not marketing. Taste that beer next to the same style from older hops and the difference is often obvious.
Hops are a farm product first

Wet hop beer is a useful reminder that hops are a crop, picked once a year and perishable like any other. Everything about pellets, freezers and nitrogen packing exists to stretch that single harvest across twelve months and thousands of kilometres.

For your next taproom visit, ask the brewer when the hops in their pale ale were harvested and how they are stored. Most brewers enjoy the question. The answer will tell you more about the beer in your glass than the hop names on the board.
faqs: What is a wet hop beer?
A beer brewed with hops that have not been dried, usually used within a day of picking. It tastes greener and fresher than beer made with pellets.
Is fresh hop beer the same as wet hop beer?
Often, but not always. Some brewers use fresh hop for hops kilned only days earlier rather than used completely undried.
Why are there no wet hop beers in India?
India grows almost no hops commercially. Wet hops spoil in a day or two, so imported hops cannot arrive in time.
When are wet hop beers released?
Soon after the harvest, which is late August and September in the northern hemisphere and roughly February to April in the southern hemisphere.
